title: 11 Voice, sound and the screen reader

steps.say: This lesson shows how the companion speaks and listens, how sound reaches the speakers, and how the screen reader works. All of it runs on this computer unless a cloud voice was chosen.

steps.anchor: /* The companion's voice and ears, on this computer: speech comes from Kokoro (Piper until a voice is chosen)
steps.through: * on screen, so the voice is never the only way in. */
steps.say: Kokoro and Piper turn text into speech. whisper.cpp turns speech into text. Everything said aloud is also written on screen.
`voice_say` is how anything is spoken. It stops whatever was being said, so the newest words always win.
Speaking is a pipeline of small programs. os-speak makes the sound, os-voicefx can shape it on the way (pitch, warmth, effects), and os-play sends it to the sound card.
Listening records the microphone with os-rec into a file in /tmp.
When they stop talking, whisper.cpp writes it down in the background. The words then go to the companion as if they had been typed.
Ctrl+Space starts and stops listening, on any screen.
The sound programs themselves are here: os-audio, os-voicefx and os-speak.
os-play and os-rec are one program, os-audio, under two names.
Under them is the kernel's Intel HD Audio driver. It offers the old Linux sound devices, /dev/dsp and /dev/mixer.

steps.say: The screen reader says what has their attention, in the companion's own words. It also lists its keys: Ctrl+Alt+R turns it on or off, and Ctrl+Alt+W says where you are.

steps.say: Its keys are read here, early in every frame, before anything else sees them. Any other key cuts it off.
It speaks through `voice_read`, a plain version of `voice_say`: no tone, and it works even when the companion's talking is turned off.
